To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the domestic wheat price effects are stronger in Russia than in Ukraine.
export controls have a dampening effect on domestic prices and that this effect is stronger in the regions with direct access to export markets.

(i) the 2010 Russian wheat export ban had a pronounced dampening effect on domestic wheat prices in the major wheat producing regions, (ii) the export ban was effective in dampening wheat prices in the regions with direct access to world markets, and (iii) the export ban had only small effects on wheat prices in the rest of the country.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether and how extreme weather conditions in large exporting countries affect domestic prices and the domestic market in the short run.
a better understanding of regional price effects of export controls and the functioning of export bans in a large country.

the question of how the Russian and Ukrainian governments can best design wheat export controls in order to minimize negative domestic price effects and to maximize export revenues in the event of harvest failures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the domestic price effects of export controls in the case of Russia and Ukraine are rather strong and that the export controls have been successful in dampening the domestic price increase.
export controls are effective in reducing domestic wheat prices in the short-run but that the magnitude of the price dampening effects varies across regions.
export controls in Russia have been effective in dampening wheat prices, while the export ban in Ukraine has not had a major impact on domestic prices.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
export bans are an effective instrument for price stabilisation in large countries, but the effectiveness depends on the regional structure of the country and the export ban design.
export controls in Russia are effective and have significant domestic price effects, but the regional variation is large.
export controls can be effective instruments in the short run.
The main takeaway from our work is that
regional heterogeneity of price dampening effects of export controls is a function of the degree of integration with the world market and the size of the domestic market.
regional heterogeneity in price effects of extreme events and policy measures should be considered to better understand the functioning of international grain markets.
export controls can be an effective policy instrument to dampen domestic wheat price effects in large wheat exporting countries.
